items.title: China's Shenzhou-24 spaceship docks with Tiangong space station
text: This real-time image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on Nov. 25, 2026 shows China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship docking with the Tiangong space station. China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe. The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA. The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship, which comprises Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong, will then enter the Tianhe module. The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)

JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).
The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe. The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA.

The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship, which comprises Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong, will then enter the Tianhe module. The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals.
The spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off at 8:18 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China on Wednesday. ■

items.title: Unclassified materials from CIA, intelligence office exposed in cyberattack: NYT
text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, The New York Times (NYT) reported Tuesday.

The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network designed to extract intelligence insights from publicly available, unclassified material, the report said, citing U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter. It added that classified material was not jeopardized.

Open-source intelligence can include vast amounts of commercially available data, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material, the report noted. "It can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data," it said.

The latest incident came to light following cyberattacks targeting multiple U.S. government agencies, including the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), raising concerns among U.S. intelligence officials.

NBC News reported Friday that the USDA had been targeted in a cyberattack earlier last week, with hackers gaining access to the department's system used to facilitate payments to farmers. CNN reported Friday night that the FBI is investigating a breach of its nationwide criminal information database.

Last Tuesday, the highly classified internal communications network used by the U.S. National Security Agency went down, although officials said the outage was not caused by a cyberattack. The disruption at the intelligence agency came after major technical outages affected airlines, banks and other companies across the country.  ■

items.title: Kuwait inaugurates national space research center, paving way for space agency
text: KUWAIT CITY, Nov. 24 (Xinhua) -- Kuwait on Tuesday inaugurated the Kuwait National Space Research Center at Sabah Al-Salem University City, aiming to strengthen its capabilities in space research and technology and pave the way for the establishment of a national space agency, the Kuwait News Agency reported.

Kuwait's Emir Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah inaugurated the center and expressed support for the scientific efforts of Kuwaiti researchers, voicing hope that the facility would strengthen national research capabilities, provide practical training opportunities for students and researchers, and foster interest in space sciences among younger generations.

Established through cooperation between the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences and Kuwait University, the center's research priorities include space physics, the study of Earth and other planets, satellite development and remote sensing technologies, and it is expected to lay the groundwork for a Kuwaiti space agency to oversee space research and activities in the country and coordinate Kuwait's participation in international space programs and initiatives, according to the report.
The center's future plans include developing KuwaitSat-2 and applying artificial intelligence and big data technologies to space research.
On Jan. 3, 2023, Kuwait launched its first satellite, KuwaitSat-1, developed by a team from Kuwait University with support from the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences.  ■

items.title: China extradites economic crime suspect from Russia
text: A suspect surnamed Shu was recently extradited from Russia to China in connection with a case involving more than 15 billion yuan ($2.25 billion) in allegedly illegal absorption of public deposits, the Ministry of Public Security said on Wednesday.
The extradition followed efforts by Chinese police, with assistance from the Chinese Embassy in Russia, the ministry said.

Shu allegedly solicited deposits from the public by promoting fictitious wealth management products and promising high annual returns, despite lacking approval from financial regulators and the qualifications required to accept public deposits.
Police in Yinzhou district of Ningbo, Zhejiang province, launched an investigation into Shu in October 2024.

Prosecutors approved his arrest in February 2025 on suspicion of illegally taking deposits from the public. Russian police apprehended Shu in November that year, prompting Chinese authorities to submit an extradition request.
Russia approved the request in September 2026, and Shu was extradited to China on Nov 5.

An official with the ministry's economic crime investigation bureau said the extradition demonstrated the determination of China and Russia to jointly combat crime and marked a milestone in deepening bilateral law enforcement and judicial cooperation.

Chinese police will continue to strengthen international law enforcement cooperation, bring fugitive criminal suspects to justice and protect the lawful rights and interests of the public, the official added.

items.title: Joint vocational workshops build skills across C. Asia
text: BISHKEK — Across Central Asia, students are learning to operate power systems, manage smart logistics and master railway technologies — skills increasingly coveted as the region's industries evolve.

Behind these opportunities is growing vocational education cooperation between China and Central Asia. Through joint workshops and training programs, institutions from both sides are translating technological exchanges into practical skills, helping young people prepare for emerging fields and careers.

At the Yaxin Workshop, an electric power training classroom at Osh Technological University in Kyrgyzstan, Nurkul Murzakulov, director of the university's Institute of Energy and Transport, explains electrical wiring techniques before students put their knowledge into practice.

Drawing on China's vocational education experience, Xinjiang Engineering Vocational University partnered with OshTU last year to establish the workshop, combining classroom instruction with hands-on training.
"Working with our Chinese partners is fast, convenient and highly efficient," said Zhanbolot Tursunbaev, rector of OshTU. He said practical training helps students better master their chosen fields.
In Almaty, Kazakhstan, an instructor at ALT University's laboratory demonstrates a modern warehouse logistics system to students.

The laboratory, part of the university's Luban Workshop, was jointly established by Urumqi Vocational University, Beijing JD Century Information Technology and ALT University. It offers students practical exposure to modern logistics.

"Here, students not only acquire theoretical knowledge but also gain familiarity with the operational models of modern logistics, an approach that aligns with the demands of the labor market," said Meruert Zharmagambetova, chair of the board and rector of ALT University.

For 21-year-old Dastan Abasbekov, a fourth-year student at OshTU's Institute of Energy and Transport, the opportunity to learn practical skills is a step toward realizing his ambition of contributing to Kyrgyzstan's energy development.

"China has a wealth of equipment and technology, and many of its factories and plants utilize advanced, feature-rich systems," he said, adding that he hopes to learn from Chinese experts in alternative energy and apply that knowledge back home.

items.title: Intl development experts discuss urban priorities in Shanghai
text:
By Zheng Zheng in Shanghai | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-24 14:54

More than 100 government representatives, technical experts and development partners from China and 10 other countries convened in Shanghai on Monday for RISE Week 2026, a platform aimed at turning urban resilience priorities into actionable, bankable projects.

Jointly hosted by the United Nations Development Programme and Tongji University, the event brings together delegates from nations including Cambodia, Indonesia, Kenya, Malaysia, the Maldives and Sri Lanka, alongside international organizations and financial institutions, to address escalating climate and disaster risks facing cities worldwide and seek to deepen South-South cooperation by linking local urban needs with technical expertise and financing channels.

"Good technical solutions cannot stand alone," said Xu Haoliang, UN undersecretary general and UNDP associate administrator. "To make a difference on the ground, they need to fit into national and city plans and be backed by finance. South-South and triangular cooperation can help close that gap by sharing knowledge, building catalytic partnerships and mobilizing innovative financing, so that technically sound solutions become country-led, bankable investments."

Zheng Qinghua, Party secretary of Tongji University and member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said that jointly building resilient cities of the future embodies humanity's aspirations for a better life and a shared desire for safer, more trustworthy and more reliable places to live. This requires bringing together global expertise, breaking down disciplinary barriers, strengthening research on the use of artificial intelligence in building resilient cities, and improving the quality and efficiency of urban development.

items.title: Rules drafted for textbook management
text: China has drafted a new regulation to strengthen textbook management across the entire chain, from planning and writing to review, publication, distribution, selection and use, as part of efforts to build a high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics.
The draft, formulated by the Ministry of Education and released on Monday, comprises eight chapters and 67 articles and is open for public opinion until Dec 24.

An accompanying explanation said the draft is intended to turn mature and effective practices into laws and regulations and provide a legal foundation for the high-quality development of textbook work.

The draft states that textbook work must uphold the leadership of the Communist Party of China and the socialist direction of education, reflect the will of the Party and the State, and promote core socialist values.

It would establish a national textbook committee under the State Council to guide and coordinate textbook work nationwide, with provincial-level committees responsible for their respective regions. The Ministry of Education would take the lead in national textbook work, while other departments would share responsibility.

The draft sets strict requirements for textbook content, saying textbooks must be politically sound, scientifically accurate and suitable for teaching. They may not violate Party and State policies, go against public order and good morals, or contain commercial advertisements or links to commercial activities. Textbooks may not be published, printed or distributed with advertisements or bundled supplementary materials.

It also tightens qualifications for textbook writers and publishers, requires chief editors to take responsibility for all content, and calls for timely revisions when major theoretical or practical developments occur or when curricula and teaching standards change. Writers would also be required to seek feedback from teachers, students and experts.

A national review system would be applied to all textbooks, with greater emphasis on political vetting. Reviewers must meet relevant qualifications and may not review textbooks they helped write or revise. They must also recuse themselves in cases involving conflicts of interest.
National curriculum textbooks for primary and secondary schools would be approved by the Ministry of Education, while local curriculum textbooks would be approved by provincial education departments.

The draft also addresses textbook pricing and distribution. Textbook prices should follow the principle of covering costs while allowing modest profits, and primary and secondary school textbooks must arrive before the start of classes.

It requires selected foreign textbooks to comply with relevant State regulations and undergo review and oversight to ensure correct orientation, scientific accuracy and advanced applicability. At the same time, it calls for stronger international exchanges and cooperation to promote high-quality Chinese textbooks abroad.

items.title: Shenzhou mission to conduct 90 sci-tech space tests
text: The Shenzhou XXIV mission will carry out 90 scientific experiments and technological tests aboard the Tiangong space station, the China Manned Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

The experiments and tests will cover space life sciences, space materials science, microgravity fluid physics and combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine, and cutting-edge aerospace technologies, said Zhang Jingbo, a senior engineer and spokesman for the agency, during a news conference held at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

As part of space life science experiments, the crew will build vascular organ chips and multi-type organ-on-a-chip devices to study how the space environment affects key physiological processes such as vascular aging, aiming to develop new strategies for preventing and treating age-related conditions, he said.

Zhang noted that the Shenzhou XXIII crewmembers have already made significant findings in this field. Their multi-omics research has revealed that spaceflight reduces the differentiation efficiency of human-induced primordial germ cells by about 50 percent, he said.

It has also identified the key pathways through which germ cells adapt to space conditions, including extracellular matrix regulation, cytoskeleton remodeling, translation control and lipid metabolism, he added.

In space materials science research, the Shenzhou XXIV astronauts will focus on the in-orbit fabrication and performance control of ultrahigh-temperature niobium-silicon intermetallic compounds and calcium-silicon multicomponent bioglass, as well as scientific studies of monocrystalline silicon and perovskite materials, Zhang said.

He noted that the Shenzhou XXIII mission produced China's first millimeter-scale deep-ultraviolet nonlinear optical crystal — potassium beryllium fluoroborate — aboard the space station. The microgravity environment significantly improved the crystal's growth quality, laying an important material foundation for high-power deep-ultraviolet laser devices.

In the field of space medicine, experiments under the Space Human Research Program will continue, Zhang said. The program will include mining multi-omics data to map the human spaceflight multi-omics atlas, quantify changes in behavioral capabilities during long-haul missions, and explore the mechanisms underlying brain function, he said.

Zhang noted that the Shenzhou XXIII astronauts have introduced advanced detection technologies, including continuous muscle imaging and intelligent quantitative assessment, in-orbit detection of multiple proteins from trace amounts of whole blood, and an AI-powered multimodal exercise-load evaluation model.
These technologies enable noncontact physiological monitoring and objective fatigue assessment, he added.

In the field of aerospace technology, the Shenzhou XXIV mission will test key technologies for a chemical-electric hybrid propulsion system featuring multiple operating modes and novel ionic liquid propellants.

items.title: Households encouraged to get smart
text: Beijing's latest efforts to boost consumption have targeted smart homes, pairing trade-in subsidies and interest-rate relief with mandatory interoperability rules to encourage households to buy not just single gadgets but entire connected home setups.

The policy package — the Action Plan for Promoting Smart Home Consumption, jointly issued in September by the Ministry of Commerce, the National Development and Reform Commission and six other government departments — combines direct fiscal funding, subsidized consumer financing, and binding national technical standards to overhaul how smart home systems are built, sold and installed.

Rather than relying solely on single-appliance rebates, the plan lays out seven concrete measures spanning high-quality supply, industry standards, consumer support, elderly-friendly products, recycling, community services, and fiscal and financial support.

Experts note that the plan is designed to unlock household demand, raise product and service quality, accelerate unified industry standards, and strengthen the competitiveness of companies at home and abroad.
Compared with previous policies, the new plan places greater emphasis on whole-home smart systems and scenario-based consumption, said Lou Feipeng, a researcher at the Postal Savings Bank of China.

Wang Peng, a researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, added that by linking subsidies, financial services, recycling and community services, the plan could lower barriers to household purchases while helping remove bottlenecks in product delivery and long-term use.
The policy comes as China continues to address weak domestic demand and promote a shift in consumption from scale expansion toward quality upgrading.

According to data from the Ministry of Commerce, the country's consumer goods trade-in programs generated 1.1 trillion yuan ($161.9 billion) in sales in the first half of 2026, benefiting consumers on 150 million occasions. Home appliance trade-ins reached 63.27 million units, while purchases of digital and smart products totaled 79.1 million units.

On the demand side, the action plan authorizes local authorities to determine eligible smart home product categories and subsidy standards based on local conditions and in line with China's 2026 consumer goods trade-in policy, while coordinating support specifically for whole-home smart systems.

At the same time, financial institutions are directed to expand consumer finance products for home furnishing and renovation, apply the fiscal interest-subsidy policy for personal consumption loans, and increase lending for smart home purchases.
Trade-in subsidies directly reduce the prices consumers pay, while interest subsidies lower the cost to households of financing the remaining purchase amount, Lou said.

The combination of the two could ease the burden of the relatively large upfront expenditure required for a whole-home smart project, Lou added. "It could enable a household that had planned to replace only one product to include installation, a control system and other devices in the same order."
The expansion of demand would also affect corporate investment and production, according to Wang.

items.title: Shenzhou XXIV makes historic Chinese-Pakistani crewed spaceflight
text: The Shenzhou XXIV, the first joint spaceflight including both Chinese and foreign astronauts, launched on Wednesday morning, carrying two Chinese crewmembers and Pakistan's first astronaut to the Tiangong space station.

As the countdown ended at 8:18 am, the 58-meter Long March 2F carrier rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center with a deafening roar from its first-stage engines. Its blazing orange exhaust illuminated the dawn over the Gobi Desert in northwestern China.

At the moment of ignition, mission commander Major General Tang Hongbo, spaceflight engineer Colonel Wu Yi, and payload specialist Wing Commander Muhammad Zeeshan Ali saluted their respective countries. The moment was broadcast live worldwide.
This marks Tang's third spaceflight and the first for Wu and Ali.

items.title: The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
text: Zhong Weiting’s wife recently bought him a pair of trousers with four front pockets. They’re for the little metal objects he carries around — things that spin, slide, click, or flip open, some made from titanium and costing thousands of yuan.
Each day, he picks a few from a plastic organizer originally bought for socks. He plays with them in elevators, in his car, and at his desk, switching to quieter models when other people are around.

For Zhong, 32, they help relieve stress and keep his restless hands occupied. “I like the sounds they make, and knowing exactly how they’ll respond gives me a sense of certainty,” he tells Sixth Tone. “I feel a kind of electric tingling in my fingertips.”

For all their elaborate mechanisms, they’re just toys to fiddle with. And Zhong, an export salesman in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen who began collecting only in November 2025, already owns 25, including one he bought this month for 2,199 yuan ($330).

Across China, the toys have found a growing following under the name EDC, short for “everyday carry,” a term borrowed from an online subculture centered on practical gear such as pocketknives and flashlights. On social media, they’re also dubbed “cyber walnuts,” after the traditional Chinese pastime of rolling a pair of walnuts in the hand.

Among the most popular designs are sliders, known in China as “push cards,” whose metal plates produce a series of tactile clicks as they slide against each other. Some toys mimic the motion of revealing a playing card or recreate the sharp tap of a telegraph key, with adjustable resistance and sound on more elaborate models.

Basic models sell for less than 100 yuan, while stainless steel versions typically cost 300 to 500 yuan. Limited editions made from rarer metals or featuring elaborate designs can run into the thousands.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, online sales of EDC toys tracked by consulting firm Meritco Databank rose 55.5% to more than 45 million yuan, with nearly 500,000 toys sold, up 78% year on year.

The vast majority of the trade, however, still takes place within collector circles. While a few large brands sell openly on popular e-commerce platforms, smaller makers rely on private groups on Chinese super app WeChat to announce new releases, sometimes limited to just a few dozen pieces.

At an EDC exhibition in Beijing in October, organizer Fu Chunjun told domestic media that the community has a name for its growing obsession: the “men’s version of Pop Mart,” the Chinese collectible-toy company known for its blind boxes.
But when Zhong shows his latest purchases to friends, few understand the appeal. “They think, why should a plastic or stainless steel gadget sell for 500 yuan?” he says.
To buy a toy from one vendor at Shanghai’s EDC exhibition in April, Guo Songhao first had to draw one of two jokers from a deck of 21 playing cards.

He drew the big joker, securing a limited-edition knuckle roller, a small metal toy designed to be rolled and flipped between the fingers. “My luck was pretty good that day,” the 25-year-old Shanghai-based engineer tells Sixth Tone.

items.title: A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
text: A Shanghai university is now giving each student and staff member up to 100 million AI tokens a week, saying that it hopes to make tokens a standard teaching resource equal to books, lab equipment, and databases.

University members may use the tokens to access a range of AI models and tools after signing in to the university website with their campus ID, as announced by Shanghai University of Finance and Economics’ (SUFE) official WeChat account on Nov. 21.
Tokens are the smallest pieces of information that AI models can process. Students can use them to debug code, clean data, conduct research, and even build their own AI agents.

China’s daily token consumption hit roughly 500 trillion in June, nearly four times that of December 2025. State-owned telecommunications carriers now sell token plans to consumers, with China Telecom’s cheapest plan costing 9.9 yuan ($1.50) a month for 10 million tokens — a 10th of SUFE’s weekly, per-person limit.
SUFE is the latest Chinese university to provide computing power and free token quotas to students and staff as a public resource, a trend that began earlier this fall.

Starting this September in Beijing, Tsinghua University began offering each student and staff member 1,000 yuan in “computing vouchers,” while Peking University offers a year of free access to Qoder, a cross-LLM AI coding assistant, and 3,000 credits a month. In the central Hunan province, Hunan University students receive 2 million tokens a day. Shanghai’s Tongji University also launched its own plan in October, giving students and faculty 100 million tokens a week.

“In the past, when you’d say a school had good infrastructure, you’d be referring to its gym and library,” Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, told domestic media. “Going forward, computing platforms, LLM data centers, and high-powered internet may be the important infrastructure of schools in the future.”

However, education researchers also report concerns that access to free tokens may fuel “idle teaching,” where teachers create assignments using AI and students submit AI-generated answers, creating a loop in which the work is completed but no real learning takes place.

“Measuring the value of token use is not about how many tokens are actually consumed but what kind of learning they advance in students,” Zhang Duanhong, director of the Center for Educational Policy Research at Tongji University, told domestic media.

items.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
text: “Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.
“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.
“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.
(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

items.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
text: Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.
In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
text: Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.
The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.
Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
text: For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

items.title: China sets new record in deep oil well casing replacement in Xinjiang region
text: The Xinjiang Oilfield, a major oil production base in northwestern China, belonging to the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) has announced that it has completed a deep underground casing replacement trial at a depth of 1,819 meters, setting a new domestic record and marking progress in technologies designed to repair aging oil wells and extend their service life, the China News Service reported Saturday.

The expanded field trial was recently completed at a Gobi Desert drilling site in the Luliang oilfield, with the operation successfully reconnecting 1,819 meters of casing and completing cementing work in the space between the casing and the surrounding wellbore.

The achievement extends the limits of a technique developed by the oilfield to tackle severe damage to underground well casings, which can otherwise make wells difficult to maintain and continue operating.

In an oil well, steel casing pipes are installed inside the drill hole to support the well walls and provide a stable passage for extracting oil or injecting water. Over years of operation, however, these pipes can corrode, become deformed or break, potentially restricting the well's internal passage and disrupting production.

At the Xinjiang Oilfield, located in the Junggar Basin in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, prolonged exposure to highly mineralized water and the gradual deformation of water-absorbing mudstone formations have contributed to increasingly serious casing damage, including large sections suffering leakage and broken pipes.

Conventional repair methods, such as plugging damaged sections, may only address the immediate leakage without removing the underlying damaged casing. Meanwhile, traditional casing replacement techniques used in shallower sections are not well suited to the complicated conditions encountered deeper underground.

To address the problem, researchers at the Xinjiang Oilfield's Oil Production Technology Research Institute developed a deep open-hole casing replacement technique in 2025. The approach involves removing damaged casing sections and installing replacement pipes, aiming to restore the wellbore to its original internal diameter rather than simply sealing the damaged areas.

An initial field trial was successfully conducted in October 2025 at Well 1424, operated by the Baikouquan Oil Production Plant. The operation replaced casings at a depth of 996 meters and accomplished 809 meters of open-hole casing milling, setting two domestic records at the time.
Building on the experience, the research team continued refining the technique in 2026, focusing on several challenges that had affected the efficiency and safety of deep underground operations.

These included difficulties in milling long unsupported sections of casing, the risk of tools becoming stuck when working along the edge of the casing, and the time-consuming process of cutting and retrieving damaged pipes at greater depths.

items.title: Trump proposes new tariffs on China, Europe and other trade partners
Trump administration to introduce new tariffs on China, EU and other major trading partners
text: The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.

The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, while also raising import taxes on goods from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base," Ambassador Jamieson Greer, the U.S. Trade Representative, said in a statement.

The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan.
In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline.

The planned tariffs would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.

The White House moved to implement the tariffs despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters about rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.

The Associated  Press

items.title: In backing Nvidia’s Huang, Trump deals his China hawks a setback
China sends first Pakistani astronaut into space
text: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS, along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

“Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking,” Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian. “Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket. There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is also due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday, footage showed, and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging, but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to complete another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronout.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Trump announces new tariffs, undeterred by midterms defeat
US Targets China, EU With New Tariffs Citing Overcapacity
text: The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

The rate for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement .

items.title: Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for China, EU and More, Citing Unfair Practices
Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
text: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a new wave of tariffs on the European Union, China and other trade partners, the result of a probe into what it says are unfair manufacturing practices.

Some of the proposals include tariffs of at least 20% on China, which would match an agreement reached with the White House. But the duties could reach up to 40% if talks between the two countries fail.
The United States’ current trade truce with China was recently extended and is set to expire in January.

The tariffs will be implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that the White House has relied upon more frequently for trade authority ever since the Supreme Court blocked many of Trump’s 2025 country-specific tariffs, imposed under a different authority.

Wednesday’s announcement came less than a month after Trump’s tariff policies — and the inflation they fueled — contributed to Republicans’ sweeping losses in the midterm elections. Inflation hit 3.7% in September, driven primarily by energy prices, but also by higher prices of goods.

In announcing the details of the new duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the overall rates applied to each trading partner would not surpass levels that were previously agreed to as part of bilateral framework trade deals.
“When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” Greer said on CNBC.
“So what we’re proposing today are actually a set of targeted tariffs to respond to this problem of excess capacity,” he added.
For example, Trump agreed to cap tariffs on E.U. imports at 15% as part of a deal reached in 2025. On Wednesday, the trade representative reiterated that cap.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for the case of China.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this,” Greer said. “They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple of months from now.”
He said he expects that “a broad” negotiation with trading partners would follow Wednesday’s proposals.

items.title: US threatens double-digit tariffs on EU, China, 12 others after investigation
Trump prepares new round of tariffs on China, other U.S. trading partners
US plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
items.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
text: President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.

The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.

The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

items.title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
text: The U.S. has proposed new tariffs on 14 partners including China, the European Union, Japan and India, as President Donald Trump doubles down on levies, despite a large chunk of his previous duties being struck down by the Supreme Court.
The targeted economies create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors which burden or restrict American commerce, a senior U.S. official said.
The 14 partners have been notified of these actions, with neither country's tariffs exceeding rates announced as part of framework deals on reciprocal trade, the official added.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for China, which faces a 20% tariff on top of the 25% imposed in 2018 over forced technology transfers.

The new duties on the world's second-largest economy could jump to 40% if it does not hold up its end of the trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in Oct. 2025, after which tariffs on Chinese exports to the U.S. were slashed to 47%.

The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
"The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said on Wednesday before the official reports were released by the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The new levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to counter foreign trade practices deemed unfair, discriminatory, or burdensome to U.S. commerce.
CNBC earlier reported that the new tariffs would be "country specific," rather than a blanket rate, citing a source familiar with the matter.
Tariffs have been a signature of the Trump administration since the president unveiled sweeping "Liberation Day" duties in April 2025 before pausing them after a sour reaction from bond markets.
In February, the Supreme Court struck down tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Trump used Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff after the court's decision, before replacing them with levies of up to 12.5% on 60 economies under Section 301, alleging forced labor practices.

items.title: Xi's graft probe of Shanghai rising star upends traditional path to power in China
